tagline: A governor's loop through the granite, meant to be taken slowly.
intro: South of Keystone the Iron Mountain Road climbs toward the peak it is named for, through one-lane tunnels lined up so that Mount Rushmore sits framed in the far opening, and drops back on the pigtail bridges. It was built in the 1930s under the direction of Peter Norbeck. To do the scenery justice, he said, drive no more than 20 miles an hour, and to do it full justice, get out and walk.

The loop runs on through Custer State Park, home to some 1,400 bison, and comes back north on the Needles Highway, finished in 1922 among granite spires that engineers said no road could get through. Norbeck had marked its course on foot and on horseback.

moments.title: Iron Mountain Road
moments.text: At the top of the climb, on the summit of Iron Mountain, a small memorial to Norbeck stands beside the road he laid out for slow driving.

moments.title: Needles Eye Tunnel
moments.text: Blasted through sheer granite beside the Needle's Eye, a spire opened up by wind, rain, freezing and thawing, the tunnel is eight feet wide.

moments.title: Sylvan Lake
moments.text: Theodore Reder dammed Sunday Gulch Creek to make it in 1891. A 2007 Hollywood film set it directly behind Mount Rushmore. It is five miles southwest.

practical: The Needles Highway closes to vehicles with the first snow and does not reopen until April 1 or later. Its tunnels are as narrow as 8 feet wide and 9 feet 9 inches high. The Iron Mountain Road also closes at times in winter.
